What to do next

Ordered by viewers at stake. Every chart says what kind of evidence it is: hover the badge. An observed figure is counted, not compared, and claims no cause. A correlation means two things move together on this channel, which is not the same as one causing the other.

  1. 1 This channel ~9K viewers at stake

    Stop shipping "DIY ___", or repackage the premise.

    This shape underperforms the channel's own median.

    What would make this wrong

    A weak format is not always a weak idea — it can be a weak package on a sound premise. Check the thumbnails and titles before retiring the shape itself.

  2. 2 Measured law ~2K viewers at stake

    Cut the intro. Open on what the thumbnail showed.

    The opening is this channel's biggest single loss.

    What would make this wrong

    Some opening loss is unavoidable: people who clicked the wrong thing leave whatever you do. Only the gap over a quarter is addressable.

Also checked, no action needed (4)
  • Ending: 3.8% of those still watching at 90% leave before the card. Under the 20.0% worth fixing.
  • Length: 52.5% against 45.8% at halfway. A 6.7% gap, too small to act on.
  • Cadence: 0.99x on rhythm against 1.00x off it. Too close to call.
  • Formats: 7 run between 0.75x and 1.30x. Working as intended.

Built from 40 videos with retention data. "Viewers at stake" is an estimate, not a forecast.

Window: the 40 most recent uploads, not all 295. Advice is about the channel being run now.

1 of 2 actions rest on this channel alone. No cross-channel measurement backs them yet.

Video wall

Each badge is the video's outlier score — its first-28-day views against the median of the uploads nearest it in time. 1.00× is typical for this channel at that point; 2×+ is a breakout; below 0.5× underperformed. Compared against contemporaries rather than the whole catalogue, because a video from before the channel grew would otherwise always look like a failure. Median, not average, so one breakout can't drag the baseline.

Formats

The repeatable shapes this channel publishes, written as templates. A format is a shape a viewer recognises as “another one of those” — so two videos belong together when they make the same promise, even if they share no words. Ordered by how well the shape performs against the channel’s own median, not by how often it is used: a format shipped twenty times that underperforms is a habit, not a strength. The multiplier is the group’s median outlier score, measured against each video’s contemporaries. A shape marked era-bound ran in a block — most of its neighbouring uploads share the same shape, so its score compares it against itself and cannot be read as performance. Interleaving two formats over the same months is what makes them comparable.

121 of 388 videos sit in a named format · library built 2026-09-02.

What the numbers show

The channel's own record, drawn. Each chart says what kind of evidence it is: an observation is counted, a correlation is compared, and neither is a cause. Score = first-28-day views against the median of the uploads nearest in time; 1.0x is typical for the channel at that point.

Analyses

No tool outputs recorded yet.

Retention overlay

Every analysed video's retention curve on one pair of axes. Both switches are live — change what the x-axis measures, or what the colour encodes, and the same data answers a different question.

View X axis Depth Compare scroll to zoom, drag to pan
Filter Window Between and Length any Views any
Colour

Median band is the view to start from on a large catalogue. A hundred and sixty curves on one pair of axes composite into a solid mat that shows only that the channel has a lot of videos; the band draws the same data as percentile envelopes, so the middle half of the catalogue and the full 10th-to-90th spread are readable at a glance. Percentiles rather than mean and standard deviation, because retention curves are not symmetric and a couple of duds would drag a mean band below where most videos actually live. Click any title to draw that one video in gold against the envelope, which answers whether it sits inside the pack or outside it. All curves is the honest full picture and the right view once a filter has cut the set down.

% of video normalises length, so structural habits line up — a sag every video shares shows as one shared dip. Clock time lets each curve stop where its video stops, so length and endurance become visible. On the % axis the dashed white line is this channel's own median — the bar every video is judged against; clock time has no shared x, so no median is drawn. By upload date adds a third axis: each plane is one slice of the channel’s history, receding by when it was published — oldest at the back. Each plane draws the MEDIAN curve of the uploads in its window, not every video: a hundred planes land a pixel apart and stack into a solid wall, and the question is whether retention drifted, not what one video did. Median rather than mean, so a single breakout cannot speak for a whole quarter. Window narrows the set: the last N uploads holds the sample size constant and answers “has my recent work changed”, while the last N days answers “what has this channel been doing lately” and lets a quiet stretch show up as a near-empty chart rather than as a flattering handful of curves. Length and Views slide over PERCENTILES of the catalogue rather than raw numbers, because views are heavy-tailed and a linear slider would spend nine tenths of its travel between the pack and one breakout; the label always shows the real threshold. Scroll to zoom anywhere on the chart and drag to pan — the axes relabel themselves because zooming narrows the DATA shown rather than magnifying the picture, so the type and the curves stay the same weight. Double-click, or Reset, to go back.

What the colours can encode. Recency, views, outlier score and retention at the halfway mark come straight off the record. Average view duration and watch time are DERIVED from the stored curve — its mean is the average share watched, so multiplying by runtime gives the duration and multiplying that by views gives the hours — which means they will not match Studio to the second, because the stored curve is sampled once per percent. A video the chosen metric was never measured for is drawn grey rather than mid-ramp, and the ramp says how many. There is deliberately no returning-viewer encoding: that split is not fetched by any run here, and an option that quietly ranked on something else would be worse than its absence.

Compare draws a reference curve against this channel's own: the median retention curve of every tracked channel, and of the channels in the same confirmed niche once ten or more of them carry curves. Each channel contributes ONE curve (its own median), so a channel with six hundred analysed uploads counts the same as one with twelve, and the line is a statement about the fleet rather than about its largest member. Reference curves live on the % axis only, like the channel median, because clock time has no shared x. The maker-build reference is withheld: 9 of 10 channels with curves.

What works inside the videos

No category on this channel had a consistent effect. Every group below is a coin flip: the beats recur, but how the audience reacts to them does not.

Each bar is the group's median effect against a typical flagged moment of the same kind at the same point in the video. Zero is ordinary. Comparing within kind on purpose: a drop loses audience by definition, so measuring one against the whole curve would only restate the label the analysis had already given it. Observed counted on this channel

These are moments the analysis FLAGGED — places where retention moved unusually — not every time each beat occurs. So a row says which way that beat goes when it moves the needle and by how much, not that it always does this.
